candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 51 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 52 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 53 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 54 not required. 55

candidates.statement: FDA encourages specific activities regarding neonates. Under PREA, if a sponsor does not plan 173 to study an investigational drug in neonates, the rationale and supporting data explaining why the 174 drug is not appropriate for use in this population should be included in the iPSP. 28 Under the 175 BPCA, similar rationale and supporting data explaining why the investigational drug is not 176 appropriate for use in this population should be included in the proposed pediatric study request 177 (PPSR) if a sponsor does not plan to study the drug in neonates. When FDA issues a WR that 178 does not include studies in neonates, the WR must state the rationale for not including 179 neonates. 29 See sections IV.A.1., Description of the Written Request, and IV.B., How to Obtain 180 a Written Request, as well as the draft guidance for industry Pediatric Drug Development Under 181 the Pediatric Research Equity Act and the Best Pharmaceuticals for Children Act: Scientific 182 Considerations 30 for more information regarding clinical studies in neonates. 183
candidates.context: The complex medical state of neonates makes it critical to evaluate drugs specifically for their 165 use. However, FDA is aware that studies in neonates present special challenges, including the 166 short time period to conduct studies during the neonatal period (e.g., birth through 27 days 167 corrected gestational age), the differences in neonatal physiology that may affect dose and 168 endpoint selection, as well as ethical issues that may be age-specific. Under PREA, studies in 169 neonates may be required. However, it is possible that partial waivers for this and other specific 170 age groups might be appropriate under certain circumstances. 27

candidates.statement: Under PREA, sponsors are required to conduct pediatric studies “using appropriate formulations 302 for each age group” for which the assessment or investigation is required. 45 However, FDA may 303 grant a partial waiver if a sponsor is unable to develop an age-appropriate formulation after 304 reasonable attempts to do so. 46 (See discussion of waivers in section III.D., Waivers and 305 Deferrals Under PREA.) candidates.statement: A WR is a document issued by FDA requesting submission of a study or studies intended to 623 provide meaningful health benefits in the pediatric population. The WR specifies the elements 624 of the study or studies that the sponsor or application holder must complete to qualify for 625 pediatric exclusivity. 89 FDA can issue a WR at the request of an interested party or on its own 626 initiative. Completion of studies described in a WR is voluntary. 90 FDA does not limit issuance 627 of a WR to a specific drug product, and the WR can result in only one 6-month period of 628 pediatric exclusivity for that sponsor, as described in section IV.F., Attaching the Period of 629 Pediatric Exclusivity After a Determination That a Drug Qualifies for Pediatric Exclusivity. 630 FDA’s authority to issue a WR extends to use of an active moiety for indications that may 631 produce health benefits in the pediatric population, regardless of whether the indications have 632 been previously approved in adults. 91

candidates.statement: The BPCA provides FDA with discretion to determine whether to issue, and the appropriate 702 scope of, WRs based on the information that “may produce health benefits” in the pediatric 703 population. 95 In light of the data on pediatric labeling changes pursuant to the BPCA and/or 704 PREA, FDA believes WRs should be reserved for those sponsors who conduct additional 705 pediatric studies — beyond what is required under PREA — that may produce health benefits in 706 children. Thus, upon finalization of this guidance, FDA does not expect to issue WRs solely for 707 studies or planned studies that are required under PREA. In general, FDA expects that a WR 708 that includes studies or planned studies required under PREA will also include additional 709 indications or populations. If there are no additional studies for indications or populations that 710 may produce health benefits in the pediatric population beyond the studies or planned studies 711 required under PREA, then FDA does not expect to issue a WR for that drug. For example, if a 712 sponsor has an iPSP that includes a plan for deferred studies of a drug for pediatric juvenile 713 idiopathic arthritis (pJIA), FDA does not expect to issue a WR solely for studies of pJIA in the 714 same pediatric population. However, if FDA determines that this drug may produce health 715 benefits in pediatric systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA), and there are no studies or 716 planned studies required under PREA for this indication, then it may be appropriate for FDA to 717 issue a WR for pediatric studies for both pJIA and sJIA. 718
